Connectivity Clustering with Predicted Groups

Source: vignettes/connectivity-clustering.Rmd
connectivity-clustering.Rmd

This vignette clusters a set of related Aedes neurons by their connectivity using coconatfly’s cf_cosine_plot(). Cosine clustering compares neurons by the partners they share, and those partners must first be grouped, so that e.g. two neurons that each contact a different member of the same partner cell type still count as similar.

In well annotated datasets partners are grouped by cell type. Most aedes neurons do not yet have a type, so we compare two alternatives:

  • group: the curated group (see aedes_set_group()).
  • pgroup: the predicted group from aedes_predict_group(), which uses the first available of cell type, curated group and NBLAST cluster.

The chunks below need FlyTable and CAVE access. They are evaluated when the pkgdown website is built; elsewhere saved results are shown instead (see Rerunning this vignette).

library(aedes)
library(coconatfly)
library(dplyr)
register_aedes_coconat()

Quick start

Once register_aedes_coconat() has been called, coconatfly metadata for aedes neurons includes a pgroup column, so you can simply choose the grouping column:

cf_cosine_plot(cf_ids(aedes = "group:36155"), group = "group")
cf_cosine_plot(cf_ids(aedes = "group:36155"), group = "pgroup")

Fetch the connectivity once

As an example we use the 12 untyped visual projection neurons in group 36155. Rather than letting cf_cosine_plot() fetch connectivity each time, we fetch a connection table once with group = FALSE and then cluster it with different grouping columns.

ids <- cf_ids(aedes = "group:36155")
cf_meta(ids) %>% select(id, serial_id, side, group, nblast_group)
#>                    id serial_id side group nblast_group
#> 1  648518347546516862     36155    R 36155        36155
#> 2  648518347589781091     36156    L 36155        36155
#> 3  648518347560355394     36159    R 36155        36155
#> 4  648518347544524186     36160    R 36155        36155
#> 5  648518347553146126     36161    L 36155        36155
#> 6  648518347592422420     36164    L 36155        36155
#> 7  648518347480058719     36165    L 36155        36155
#> 8  648518347482226372     36167    R 36155        36155
#> 9  648518347513818908     36180    L 36155        36155
#> 10 648518347558714862     38437    L 36155        36155
#> 11 648518347650879288     38438    R 36155        36155
#> 12 648518347592047808     38439    R 36155        36155

x <- multi_connection_table(ids, partners = c("in", "out"), threshold = 5,
                            group = FALSE)
#> Warning in fafbseg::cam_meta(ids = ids, ignore.case = ignore.case, fixed = fixed, : Dropping 1 rows containing duplicate root_ids!
#> You can inspect all 2 rows with duplicate ids by doing:
#> attr(df, 'duprows')
#> on your returned data frame (replacing df as appropriate).

Partner neurons without a label in the chosen column cannot act as shared features and are dropped. We can check what fraction of the partner synapses each column covers:

cov <- x %>%
  group_by(partners) %>%
  summarise(type = sum(weight[!is.na(type)]) / sum(weight),
            group = sum(weight[!is.na(group)]) / sum(weight),
            pgroup = sum(weight[!is.na(pgroup)]) / sum(weight)) %>%
  mutate(across(-partners, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
cov
#>   partners  type group pgroup
#> 1   inputs 0.002 0.161  0.161
#> 2  outputs 0.008 0.613  0.621

Cell types cover under 1% of partner synapses, so group = "type" is not useful here. Using pgroup rather than group raises coverage of output synapses from 61% to 62%. Input coverage stays low because most of the input partners are not yet in FlyTable at all.

Cluster by curated group 

cf_cosine_plot(x, group = "group", labRow = "{side}_{serial_id}")
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["outputs"]], inputcol =
#> "pre_key", : Dropping: 1092/1715 neurons representing 11475/29629 synapses due
#> to missing ids!
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["inputs"]], inputcol =
#> groupcol, : Dropping: 4259/4477 neurons representing 49907/59475 synapses due
#> to missing ids!

Cluster by predicted group 

cf_cosine_plot(x, group = "pgroup", labRow = "{side}_{serial_id}")
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["outputs"]], inputcol =
#> "pre_key", : Dropping: 1078/1715 neurons representing 11240/29629 synapses due
#> to missing ids!
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["inputs"]], inputcol =
#> groupcol, : Dropping: 4256/4477 neurons representing 49877/59475 synapses due
#> to missing ids!

At the time of writing (September 2026) both groupings split the 12 neurons into six left/right pairs, which is reassuring. With pgroup the extra partner information gave a crisper result: 36155/36156 and 38437/38439 separated cleanly into two pairs rather than forming one loosely resolved cluster of four.

How the predicted group is defined

aedes_predict_group() returns ids that all live in the serial_id namespace, taking the first of these that is available:

  1. type: the smallest serial_id among neurons of that type (a trailing ? is ignored, as are uninformative types listed in badtypes).
  2. group: the curated group.
  3. nblast_group: clusters of the form CNNNNN or NNNNN, where NNNNN is the smallest serial_id in the cluster (surrounding whitespace and a trailing ? are ignored). Any other value is ignored, so a bad cluster can be struck out by prefixing it with X (e.g. XC12345) without deleting the information.

Neurons with none of these get NA and are dropped as partners. With singletons = TRUE they instead fall back to their own serial_id, i.e. a group of one, so that every partner in FlyTable keeps its connectivity as a feature, behaving like group = FALSE for that neuron. This is off by default because a singleton partner can only be shared by neurons on the same side of the brain, which tends to pull left/right homologues apart.

Because type-derived ids use the smallest serial_id among the rows supplied, they can depend on which neurons are in the table. Within one cf_cosine_plot() call the partner metadata for each direction is fetched together, so the ids are consistent where it matters.

You can also compute predicted groups yourself, e.g. to use a custom badtypes list:

x$pgroup2 <- aedes_predict_group(x, badtypes = c(NA, "", "undefined"))
cf_cosine_plot(x, group = "pgroup2", labRow = "{side}_{serial_id}")
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["outputs"]], inputcol =
#> "pre_key", : Dropping: 1078/1715 neurons representing 11240/29629 synapses due
#> to missing ids!
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["inputs"]], inputcol =
#> groupcol, : Dropping: 4256/4477 neurons representing 49877/59475 synapses due
#> to missing ids!

Advanced: splitting ipsilateral and contralateral connectivity

Grouping partners by pgroup ignores which side of the brain they are on, so a neuron that contacts the left-side members of a partner group looks the same as one that contacts the right-side members. We do not normally want to separate partners by side (after all, this is precisely how connectivity clustering can identify left-right homologues), but for bilateral neurons it may be useful to distinguish ipsilateral from contralateral connectivity. This could be important e.g. for bilateral inhibitory neurons involved in steering.

To keep the side information, we can give each partner group two labels, depending on whether the partner is on the same side of the brain as the query neuron (NNNNNi, ipsilateral) or on the opposite side (NNNNNc, contralateral).

As an example we use the 19 lateral horn local neurons (class LHLN) in groups 30221 (16 bilateral, subclass BR) and 30225 (3 unilateral, subclass IR). These were originally annotated as two groups but do not split cleanly along those lines. Connections among the query neurons themselves can dominate the comparison when they are heavily interconnected, as these are, so we drop those first.

ids_lh <- cf_ids(aedes = "group:30221|30225")
x_lh <- multi_connection_table(ids_lh, threshold = 5, group = FALSE)

qkeys <- keys(ids_lh)
qside <- cf_meta(ids_lh) %>% select(query_key = key, query_side = side)

x_lr <- x_lh %>%
  # drop connections among the query neurons
  filter(!(pre_key %in% qkeys & post_key %in% qkeys)) %>%
  # the query neuron is postsynaptic for inputs, presynaptic for outputs
  mutate(query_key = if_else(partners == "inputs", post_key, pre_key)) %>%
  left_join(qside, by = "query_key") %>%
  mutate(
    lat = case_when(!side %in% c("L", "R") | !query_side %in% c("L", "R") ~ NA,
                    side == query_side ~ "i",
                    .default = "c"),
    # keep NA so that unlabelled partners are dropped, not pooled
    pgroup_lr = if_else(is.na(pgroup) | is.na(lat), NA, paste0(pgroup, lat)))
x_lr
#> # A tibble: 281 × 52
#>    post_id  pre_id weight supervoxel_id serial_id point_xyz side  class subclass
#>    <int64> <int64>  <int> <chr>         <chr>     <chr>     <chr> <chr> <chr>   
#>  1    6e17    6e17     93 741706516442… 11451     17815,18… R     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  2    6e17    6e17     64 755076577165… 10959     27167.48… L     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  3    6e17    6e17     63 755076577164… 10957     27182.10… L     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  4    6e17    6e17     60 742410203885… 11419     17934,17… R     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  5    6e17    6e17     54 742410203885… 11419     17934,17… R     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  6    6e17    6e17     54 742410203885… 11419     17934,17… R     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  7    6e17    6e17     54 741706516442… 11451     17815,18… R     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  8    6e17    6e17     53 755076577165… 10959     27167.48… L     cb_i… ALPN    
#>  9    6e17    6e17     50 755076577165… 10959     27167.48… L     cb_i… ALPN    
#> 10    6e17    6e17     40 755076577165… 10959     27167.48… L     cb_i… ALPN    
#> # ℹ 271 more rows
#> # ℹ 43 more variables: type <chr>, group <chr>, nblast_group <chr>,
#> #   notes <chr>, proofreader <chr>, annotator <chr>, lineage <chr>,
#> #   neuropils <chr>, status <chr>, axon_tract <chr>,
#> #   neurotransmitter_verified <chr>, neurotransmitter_verified_source <chr>,
#> #   soma_xyz <chr>, nucleus_id <dbl>, birthtime <chr>, nerve <chr>,
#> #   lrcid <chr>, synonyms <chr>, flywire_type <chr>, instance <chr>, …

multi_connection_table(group = FALSE) returns one row per connection between a query neuron and a partner, with the partner’s metadata (including side and pgroup). The partners column says whether the partner is an input or an output, and therefore whether the query neuron is in post_key or pre_key; we use that to look up the query neuron’s soma side. Comparing the two sides gives an i or c suffix for the partner’s pgroup, so each partner group becomes two separate features.

Partners with no pgroup or no L/R side must stay NA, so that they are dropped like any other unlabelled partner. Pasting a suffix onto NA would make a string such as "NAc", merging every unlabelled partner into one fake shared group that inflates similarity.

We then cluster on the new column, labelling each neuron with its curated group so we can see how the two groups mix:

cf_cosine_plot(x_lr, group = "pgroup_lr",
               labRow = "{group}_{side}_{serial_id}")
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["outputs"]], inputcol =
#> "pre_key", : Dropping: 83/195 neurons representing 701/1828 synapses due to
#> missing ids!
#> Warning in coconat::partner_summary2adjacency_matrix(x[["inputs"]], inputcol =
#> groupcol, : Dropping: 27/86 neurons representing 200/1540 synapses due to
#> missing ids!

Note that “side” means soma side. For bilateral neurons, an i partner shares the query neuron’s soma side; that says nothing about where on the query neuron the synapse is. It is worth checking how much of the connectivity the split actually affects:

lr_wt <- x_lr %>%
  filter(!is.na(pgroup_lr)) %>%
  count(partners, lat, wt = weight) %>%
  as.data.frame()
lr_wt
#>   partners lat    n
#> 1   inputs   c   21
#> 2   inputs   i 1319
#> 3  outputs   c  256
#> 4  outputs   i  871

At the time of writing (November 2026) only 277 of the 2467 synapses with labelled partners were contralateral, almost all of them outputs, so the split changes the clustering only modestly here.

Rerunning this vignette

The results above depend on the live FlyTable annotations and CAVE connectivity, so they will change as proofreading and annotation progress.

  • Website. The pkgdown GitHub Actions workflow has the necessary FlyTable and CAVE credentials and evaluates this vignette in full whenever the site is rebuilt and deploys it on every push to main (pull requests also build the site, but do not deploy it). To refresh it without a push, trigger the workflow manually from the repository’s Actions tab or with gh workflow run pkgdown.yaml.

  • Locally. With FlyTable and CAVE access set up, render the vignette with the live chunks enabled:

    Sys.setenv(AEDES_LIVE_VIGNETTES = "true")
rmarkdown::render("vignettes/connectivity-clustering.Rmd")

  • Saved results. When not evaluated live (e.g. during R CMD check or vignette("connectivity-clustering") from an installed package) the saved figures in vignettes/figures/ are shown. To refresh them, also set AEDES_SAVE_VIGNETTE_FIGURES=true when rendering locally, then update the saved coverage and weight tables and the “at the time of writing” text to match.
